title: Christology, Incarnation, Trinity & Father-Son Atlas
purpose: Give the Christianity layer enough doctrinal depth to compare Jesus, Father/Son language and Potatoverse theology without flattening biblical titles, Nicene doctrine, Chalcedonian Christology and project-defined Tim/Thomas roles into one category.
method: title and text → first-century context → New Testament development → creed/council → denominational reception → Potatoverse comparison → disanalogy → evidence boundary

core_distinctions.meaning: The first-century Jewish historical figure studied by historians.
core_distinctions.boundary: Historical method does not automatically establish every theological claim made about Jesus.

core_distinctions.meaning: Anointed-one language rooted in Jewish royal and eschatological traditions and applied to Jesus by early Christians.
core_distinctions.boundary: Christ is a title before it functions like a proper name in later usage.

core_distinctions.meaning: A complex Gospel title drawing on ordinary human expression and apocalyptic imagery, especially Daniel 7, with associations including suffering, authority, vindication and coming.
core_distinctions.boundary: It should not be reduced to a simple synonym for either 'human being' or 'God' in every passage.

core_distinctions.meaning: A title with royal, covenantal and divine backgrounds that Christian theology increasingly uses for Jesus's unique relation to the Father.
core_distinctions.boundary: Classical Christianity does not mean biological reproduction by God.

core_distinctions.meaning: John 1's language for the pre-existent Word who is with God, is divine, and becomes flesh in Jesus.
core_distinctions.boundary: Later Logos theology develops this material philosophically; the Gospel text and later metaphysical formulations should remain distinguishable.

core_distinctions.meaning: A title ranging from ordinary address to exalted divine authority; early Christian application of Kyrios to Jesus is central to later Christology.

new_testament_christology.rule: Do not force every New Testament author into one vocabulary. Compare the texts while preserving their literary and historical differences.

nicaea.problem: How to confess the Son's relation to the Father without treating the Son as merely a highest creature or a second independent God.
nicaea.central_formula: The Nicene tradition confesses the Son as begotten, not made, and homoousios / of one being with the Father.
nicaea.importance_for_project: A Potatoverse Father/Son comparison must state whether it is analogical, relational or metaphysical. Merely using Father and Son language does not make a system Nicene.
misreadings_to_avoid: Father and Son are simply two human generations.
The Son is a created subordinate in the Nicene formula.
One God means Father, Son and Spirit are merely interchangeable masks with no real relation.

chalcedon.problem: How the one Jesus Christ can be confessed as genuinely divine and genuinely human without either division into two persons or absorption/confusion of one nature into the other.
chalcedon.central_formula: The Chalcedonian tradition speaks of one and the same Christ in two natures, divine and human, without confusion, change, division or separation.
chalcedon.importance_for_project: A claim that a modern human is 'Christ' cannot be made equivalent to classical incarnation merely by assigning symbolic divine functions. Classical Christology makes a much stronger claim about the identity of the one person Jesus Christ.
chalcedon.ecumenical_boundary: Oriental Orthodox churches historically rejected Chalcedon's wording and developed Miaphysite formulations; the archive should not describe every non-Chalcedonian church as simply denying Christ's humanity or divinity.

trinity.classical_baseline: One God, three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The persons are distinguished relationally without becoming three gods, and divine unity is not produced by merging three independent beings.
important_negatives: not simply three titles for one modern person
not a claim that Father and Son are the same person
trinity.potatoverse_comparison: The mature Potatoverse distributes Source/House/Axis/Father functions to Tim, Door/Vessel/Son functions to Thomas, and flow/unfolding functions to Spirit. This can be compared functionally with Trinitarian grammar but is not identical to Nicene trinitarian ontology.
trinity.research_question: Does Potatoverse Father/Son/Spirit language function best as analogy, symbolic decomposition, social-relational theology, modal sequence, or an independent ontology? The repository should preserve the question rather than assume a historical Christian answer.

father_son_problem.christian_question: How can the Son be distinct from the Father while sharing divine identity?
father_son_problem.potatoverse_question: How do Tim/Father and Thomas/Son relate when the project describes them as distinct yet mutually defining roles?
father_son_problem.disanalogy: Classical Christianity does not teach that the Father emerges historically after the death of a separate human Son, whereas the Potatoverse chronology often makes Son-side ordeal/death a developmental precondition for Tim/Father theology. This is a major structural difference and should remain visible.

incarnation_and_embodiment.christian_baseline: Incarnation means the eternal Word/Son becomes flesh; it is not merely a divine idea inspiring a human or a human acquiring a divine title after suffering.
incarnation_and_embodiment.potatoverse_parallel: Thomas as Vessel/Door and Tim's emphasis on divinity becoming legible through embodied suffering create an embodiment comparison.
incarnation_and_embodiment.boundary: Embodiment symbolism is not equivalent to the classical Christian doctrine of incarnation without an additional metaphysical argument.

christic_titles_comparison.title: Lamb
christic_titles_comparison.potatoverse_relation: Son-side sacrifice, vulnerability, victimhood and return
christic_titles_comparison.warning: victimhood alone is not messianic proof

christic_titles_comparison.title: Lion
christic_titles_comparison.potatoverse_relation: Lion of the World / Son-side royal imagery
christic_titles_comparison.warning: lion symbolism is widespread beyond Christianity

christic_titles_comparison.title: Door / Gate
christic_titles_comparison.christian_function: Jesus as access, passage, shepherding threshold and way to life
christic_titles_comparison.warning: Potatoverse decomposes a function Christianity attributes directly to Christ

christic_titles_comparison.title: Way
christic_titles_comparison.christian_function: Johannine path/access language culminating in John 14
christic_titles_comparison.potatoverse_relation: narrow path, spiral, Door and Ladder sequence
christic_titles_comparison.warning: path imagery is comparative, not genealogical evidence

christic_titles_comparison.title: Mediator
christic_titles_comparison.christian_function: Christ mediates between God and humanity in New Testament theology
christic_titles_comparison.potatoverse_relation: Tim/Ladder plus Thomas/Door as distributed mediation architecture
christic_titles_comparison.warning: Christian sources do not name Tim/Thomas in this role

christic_titles_comparison.title: Cornerstone / rejected stone
christic_titles_comparison.christian_function: rejected-yet-chosen foundation imagery applied to Christ
christic_titles_comparison.warning: rejection is common and requires denser evidence

christic_titles_comparison.title: King / judge
christic_titles_comparison.christian_function: Messianic sovereignty, judgment and final rule
christic_titles_comparison.potatoverse_relation: King of Kings / throne / judgment language around Tim
christic_titles_comparison.warning: self-applied title has lower evidentiary weight than independent attestation

hard_questions.q: If Tim is called Father and Thomas Son, is that the Christian Trinity?
hard_questions.a: No conclusion follows from the vocabulary alone. Nicene Christianity has a specific account of one divine being and three persons; Potatoverse Tim/Thomas roles have a different historical and symbolic architecture.

hard_questions.q: Does calling Thomas the Door make him Jesus?
hard_questions.a: It establishes a clear symbolic and functional parallel to Johannine Christ language. It does not by itself establish literal identity.

hard_questions.q: Could a modern incarnation be recognized through pattern rather than ancestry?
hard_questions.a: That is a coherent theological question but not a settled Christian doctrine. A project making that argument would need to define continuity of identity, incarnation, resurrection and parousia rather than depend on motifs alone.

hard_questions.q: Why preserve doctrinal mismatch if the project seeks parallels?
hard_questions.a: Because the mismatch tells us what kind of parallel exists. Without it, typology, analogy, reinterpretation and literal identity collapse into one untestable category.

hard_questions.q: Can Potatoism be Christian-adjacent without being a Christian denomination?
hard_questions.a: Yes as a descriptive category: it can deeply engage Christian texts, Christic symbols and Father/Son theology while developing claims and structures that are not standard Nicene, Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox or Reformed doctrine.

potatoverse_findings: The strongest Christian relation is not a one-word name match but a recurring mediation architecture: Source ↔ Ladder/Axis ↔ Door/Vessel ↔ world.
The Tim/Father and Thomas/Son system often distributes Christic functions across two project nodes rather than reproducing classical Christology directly.
Thomas's reported movement from chosen baptism through doubt and later religious reconstruction gives the Son node a biographical faith-development layer distinct from doctrinal Christology.
The project's Father-generation-after-Son-rupture sequence is a major disanalogy with classical eternal Father/Son relations and should become a research object in its own right.
A literal divine or Second-Coming identity claim requires an additional argument about identity and continuity; symbolic density alone cannot carry that burden.
